description: AEGIS LABS explores rockets, UAVs, robotics and RoboWar. Led by Sarvesh Sehra, a first-year CSE (AI & DS) student at JECRC University, Jaipur, we combine hands-on engineering with software. We’re developing TerraPlan using NASA data to explore crop rotations. Join us to build, test and learn together. We welcome skills in coding, AI/data analysis, UI/UX, electronics, CAD and agriculture.
summary: TerraPlan is a crop-rotation decision-support website developed by AEGIS LABS for farmers facing changing weather and limited water. It combines NASA POWER weather history with soil category, irrigation availability, crop characteristics and farmer priorities to compare the current rotation with two alternatives. Our demonstration focuses on Jobner near Jaipur, using a hypothetical bajra–wheat farm. Each plan explains its reasoning, historical evidence, potential benefits, water gaps and questions requiring local review. Farmers can adjust priorities, explore crop timelines and test different rainfall, temperature and irrigation scenarios. TerraPlan makes the assumptions visible so farmers can discuss options with agricultural experts. It supports judgment rather than replacing it, and its crop parameters remain unverified pending local agronomic validation.
details:
TerraPlan helps farmers explore crop rotations using their existing crops and available resources. Users enter a field location, broad soil category, irrigation availability, equipment and current seasonal rotation. The application combines these inputs with historical NASA POWER records and fifteen crop profiles to generate and compare rotation options. Six adjustable priorities represent water use, forage, nitrogen fixation, erosion control, organic matter and market suitability.

The comparison retains the farmer’s current rotation alongside two alternatives. Each plan includes crop windows, historical weather markers, confidence reasons, potential benefits, information gaps and local checks. A sortable table exposes the retained rotations, while excluded combinations remain visible with reasons. What-if controls change rainfall, temperature and irrigation assumptions while evaluating the same baseline plans. Four historical agricultural years provide a sensitivity comparison.

Our Jaipur demonstration represents a hypothetical two-hectare farm near Jobner. The catalogue includes Indian mustard, barley and cluster bean with research references and explicit modelling assumptions. The website also provides a glossary, regional navigation and crop labels, an optional map, a controllable 3D field illustration, attributed crop photographs, printable screens and a downloadable decision brief.

We built the application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript ES modules, with a pure calculation engine, browser-local storage, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. The software passes 110 automated tests. Crop parameters and scoring rules remain illustrative and require local agricultural validation. Scores represent relative comparisons rather than yield or profit predictions. We have not claimed field-trial results, measured water savings or institutional endorsement. Our next steps are agronomist review, verification of actual soil and irrigation conditions, and farmer usability testing.
